story.hook: My landlord charged me for damage I inherited

punchline.text: His own welcome photo proved the crack existed before I ever had the keys.

story.script:
Three days after I moved out, my landlord sent me a photo of a cracked kitchen countertop and said he was keeping almost my entire deposit. I stared at the picture because I knew that crack. It had been there the day I moved in.

The annoying part was that I had been almost too careful with that apartment. I used cutting boards, put felt pads under appliances, and reported every tiny issue through the tenant portal. But when I searched the portal for my original move-in report, the old attachment link was dead. My landlord took that as proof that I had nothing.

He told me the repair quote was urgent and that if I wanted to dispute it, I had forty-eight hours to send evidence. Then he added that the countertop had been “perfect before my tenancy.” That sentence bothered me more than the money.

I went through my phone backups and found the move-in video I had taken while my sister helped me unpack. The crack appeared for about two seconds in the corner of the frame. It was visible, but not clear enough to make me comfortable. So I kept digging.

Then I remembered something strange from the first week. The landlord had emailed me a welcome pack with several photos showing where the water shutoff and electrical panel were located. One of those photos had been taken from the kitchen doorway. I downloaded the original attachment instead of the compressed preview.

There it was. The same crack, in the same shape, under the same light. The file metadata showed the photo was taken eleven months before I moved in.

I sent him the image and asked him to confirm that it came from his own welcome pack. He replied with one sentence: “That does not prove the condition at handover.” So I stopped arguing and opened the official deposit dispute form. I attached his original email, the file metadata, my move-in video, and the repair charge.

The next morning he called me instead of replying in writing. He said we could “save everyone time” if I accepted half the deduction. I told him I was happy to let the documented process decide.

Two days later he withdrew the entire countertop claim. He still deducted a small cleaning fee that was actually listed in my checkout report, and I accepted that.

The best part came when he sent the final deposit statement. He included the old kitchen photo again, apparently forgetting it was the exact evidence that ended his claim.

I also asked the agent to send me the original move-in condition report. It listed scuffed paint, a loose kitchen handle, and two tiny marks near the balcony door, but the crack itself had been missed. That initially worried me because it meant the checklist alone would not settle anything. Then I remembered the landlord had taken a cheerful “welcome home” photo of me holding the keys on move-in day and had texted it to me that evening. The window was clearly visible behind me.

I downloaded the original image instead of using the compressed copy in the chat. The file still contained its creation date, and when I zoomed in, the same branching crack was visible in exactly the same place. I sent the untouched photo, the message timestamp, and the checkout photo to the agent and asked them to compare the pattern rather than just the existence of damage.

The landlord replied that the image was too blurry to prove anything. The agent disagreed. They overlaid the two photos and pointed out that the three distinctive branches matched. They also noted that the welcome photo predated the start time on my tenancy agreement by several hours. Suddenly the argument was no longer about whose memory was better.

His own welcome photo proved the crack existed before I ever had the keys.
